text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Norwegian papers this morning:

- The Labour party and the Centre Party are about to come to an agreement over a new system for property tax. The new proposed system also includes calculations on the land plot. The tax is payable on properties worth over one million crowns.

- This year's and next year's wage settlements will be more difficult to push through if the crown continues to be in free float, says Svein Longva, head of the government department Statistics Norway (SSB). Longva says the talks will be a test for monetary policy, fiscal policy and wage policy.

- Costs for oil activities in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea are much higher than on the British continental shelf, says a new study by professors Oeystein Noreng and Svein Andersen at the Norwegian School of Management. The main reasons are lower competition and close ties between operators and suppliers.

- News figures from the Norwegian Shipping Association show that the number of ships under Norwegian ownership increased by 62 in 1996 and to 1,447 vessels. Two out of every three ships sail under the Norwegian flag.

- British investors account for 36 percent of foreign players on the Oslo bourse. Britain, the United States and Belgium together form 85 percent of foreign dealings in Norwegian companies, according to a new report from the exchange. Seismic company Petroleum Geo-Services, telecommunications group Alcatel STK, technology firm SensoNor and Fokus Bank have the largest overseas ownership.

- Billionaire entrepreneur Kjell Inge Roekke is believed to be the central figure behind the large buy up of 500 million crowns worth of shares in insurance company Storebrand on Friday. Storebrand head Aage Korsvold has no comment on shareholders' acitivites.

- The Norwegian financial sector is about 500 billion crowns, or 25 percent, smaller than it should be, a study comparing the sectors in Norway, Sweden and Denmark shows. One of the reasons is that Norwegian banks have sold less overseas than Swedish and Danish competition.
- Kvaerner plans to cut its workforce worldwide by 2,000. The number of Kvaerner employees rose by 2,000 in the fourth quarter last year to 56,500.

- The ownership in Norway's largest listed oil company Saga Petroleum is the most interesting question at the moment. Norsk Hydro and Statoil have around 33 percent of the voting shares in Saga. If they sell out, Saga's market capitalisation could rise to international oil company status, and it would become a buy candidate.
